Subantarctic snipe (Coenocorypha aucklandica) eggs are incubated for approximately 22 days [ab = approximately 22 days] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a period typical for small scolopacids nesting in cool subantarctic conditions. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of 13.6 grams [Wwb = 13.6 grams], a remarkably low neonatal mass that reflects the extremely altricial state of the hatchlings. This minimal birth mass is consistent with the pattern observed across other Coenocorypha species, where downy young are incapable of thermoregulation and depend entirely on brooding by the attending adult. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, measured prior to any significant water loss, is 23.5 grams [Ww0 = 23.5 grams], indicating that the embryo consumes a substantial proportion of the yolk reserves during development. Field measurements from the Auckland Islands confirm that the incubation temperature is maintained with remarkable precision by the incubating parent, despite ambient temperatures that frequently fall below freezing.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically 41 °C [T = 41 °C], fledging occurs at 54 days after hatching [tx = 54 days after hatching]. This relatively protracted nestling period is characteristic of subantarctic shorebirds, which generally exhibit slower development than their temperate counterparts, likely as an adaptive response to the unpredictable and nutrient-poor foraging environment. The fledging age represents the point at which the chick achieves sustained flight and begins to accompany the adults away from the immediate nest vicinity, although full independence is not attained for several weeks thereafter. Observations of marked individuals indicate that while flight feather maturation proceeds steadily, the young remain partially dependent on parental provisioning during the initial post-fledging phase. The transition from nestling dependency to independent foraging is a critical period during which juvenile mortality is highest, underscoring the selective pressure on rapid yet energetically feasible wing and muscle development.

Sexual maturity in the Subantarctic snipe is attained at 162 days after hatching [tp = 162 days after hatching] when maintained at a core body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This represents a comparatively rapid maturation schedule for a bird of this body size and latitude, likely facilitated by the protein-rich invertebrate diet available in the peat soils of the subantarctic islands. The point at which fledging occurs, 54 days after hatching [tx = 54 days after hatching], under the same thermal regime provides a baseline for understanding the growth trajectory, as the period between fledging and puberty is one of intensive mass gain and skeletal maturation at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. Young birds typically embark on a phase of exploratory dispersal during this interval, gradually establishing familiarity with potential breeding territories. The attainment of gonadal maturity coincides with the acquisition of full adult plumage, which in this species is cryptic and well-suited to the tussock grass habitat. Post-pubertal individuals then face the challenge of securing a nest site and a mate in a population where suitable breeding habitat is both limited and fiercely contested.

The first successful breeding event, defined as the production of a clutch, typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under an ambient thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This delay between puberty and actual first reproduction is a common feature among long-lived shorebirds and reflects the time required for territory establishment and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Females lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing a maximum of 2 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing a maximum of 2 eggs], resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year]. This low fecundity is offset by a relatively high adult survival rate and a prolonged reproductive lifespan, allowing individuals multiple breeding attempts across their lifetime. The decision to defer reproduction until the second year after hatching is thought to reduce the risk of early mortality associated with inexperience.

Longevity records for the Subantarctic snipe indicate a maximum lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] when maintained at a body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This remarkable longevity, unusual for a bird of this body size, is a hallmark of the slow life-history strategy typical of subantarctic endemics. Females attain an asymptotic adult body mass of 116 grams [Wwi = 116 grams], while the slightly smaller males reach an adult body mass of 101.2 grams [Wwi = 101.2 grams]; this modest sexual size dimorphism is consistent across all studied populations. The energy requirements for sustaining such a long life are met through a diet composed predominantly of terrestrial invertebrates, supplemented by occasional marine amphipods in coastal areas. Senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in reproductive output rather than a catastrophic failure of physiological systems, with some individuals continuing to breed successfully even in their final years. The combination of extended lifespan and low annual reproductive effort places this snipe firmly within the slow end of the avian life-history continuum.
